newsitem.title: USA: Oregon ryegrass spores tested for Karnal bunt.
newsitem.headline: Oregon ryegrass spores tested for Karnal bunt.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department scientists are testing fungus spores found in Oregon ryegrass to determine if they are Karnal bunt, a USDA official said.

Arnold Tschanz, director of USDA's National Plant Germplasm Quarantine Center, said preliminary results may be available late this month. Karnal bunt is a fungal disease that was found in U.S. wheat last year, causing wheat in several states to be placed under quarantine.
"All indications at this point are that it is the Karnal bunt organism," Tschanz said.
Oregon exports ryegrass which is planted to pastures, lawns and golf courses.
Arizona state agriculture officials discovered the suspect spores in Oregon ryegrass last month. They wrote to the U.S. Agriculture Department asking why it had not placed a quarantine on the grass.
Tests by the Arizona Department of Agriculture indicated the spores in the Oregon ryegrass were Karnal bunt, but USDA officials in Oregon said a link had not been proved.
Arizona has blocked entry of Oregon ryegrass until it has been tested free of the spores, Arizona and Oregon officials said.
"Obviously, we don't want any more spores in our state," said Keith Meyer, a spokesman for the Arizona Department of Agriculture.

The USDA last year placed Arizona wheat under quarantine after finding instances of Karnal bunt. The fungus does not pose a health risk to consumers but can affect the taste and smell of wheat and wheat-based products.
USDA officials are in the process of contaminating wheat plants with the ryegrass spores to determine if they produce Karnal bunt, Tschanz said.
Oregon officials say it is too early to link the ryegrass spores to Karnal bunt.

"If it were in the wheat we would expect the absolute same treatment they (Arizona) got," said Dan Hilburn, plant division administrator for the Oregon Department of Agriculture. "But this is a whole different host, and our wheat has turned up clean."

Hilburn said some tests have shown a similarity between the ryegrass spores and Karnal bunt. But he said the spores have been present in Oregon ryegrass since 1993 and have not migrated to wheat, raising doubt that the spores are in fact Karnal bunt.
"We are not sure what it is," said Gary Smith, USDA's plant health specialist in Oregon. "We've taken hundreds of samples of wheat and nothing came up positive."
Besides Arizona, Karnal bunt was found last year in wheat from Alabama, California, Tennessee and Texas.
